questions.q: Write the vector equation of a plane passing through the point with position vector \(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}\) and perpendicular to the vector \(4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}\).
questions.a: The vector equation is \(\mathbf{r} \cdot (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}) = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}) \cdot (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}) = 8 - 6 - 5 = -3\). So \(\mathbf{r} \cdot (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}) = -3\). A wrong answer like \(\mathbf{r} \cdot (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + 5\mathbf{k}) = 3\) reveals a sign error in the dot product computation, specifically mishandling the negative signs of the point's coordinates.

questions.q: Explain why the equation \(A(x - x_1) + B(y - y_1) + C(z - z_1) = 0\) represents a plane passing through \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) with normal direction ratios \(A, B, C\).
questions.a: The left-hand side is the dot product of the normal vector \((A, B, C)\) with the vector from \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) to \((x, y, z)\). For any point \((x, y, z)\) on the plane, this vector lies in the plane and must be perpendicular to the normal, so their dot product is zero. Substituting \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) makes each term zero, satisfying the equation. A student who says "it's just the formula" without linking to perpendicularity shows a lack of conceptual understanding of why the normal vector appears in the equation.

questions.q: Find the Cartesian equation of the plane passing through the point \((1, -2, 3)\) and perpendicular to the line with direction ratios \(2, -1, 4\).
questions.a: The normal vector to the plane is parallel to the given line, so direction ratios of the normal are \(2, -1, 4\). Using \(A(x - x_1) + B(y - y_1) + C(z - z_1) = 0\): \(2(x - 1) - 1(y + 2) + 4(z - 3) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x - 2 - y - 2 + 4z - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow 2x - y + 4z - 16 = 0\). A common error is writing \(2(x-1) -1(y-2) + 4(z-3) = 0\) by forgetting that \(y_1 = -2\) gives \(y - (-2) = y+2\). This sign mistake changes the constant term entirely.

questions.q: A plane passes through points \(A(1, 1, 0)\), \(B(2, 0, 1)\), and \(C(0, 2, 1)\). Without finding the full equation, determine whether the point \(D(1, 1, 1)\) lies on this plane.
questions.a: Vectors \(\overrightarrow{AB} = (1, -1, 1)\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC} = (-1, 1, 1)\). Their cross product \(\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = (-2, -2, 0)\) is normal to the plane. The plane equation is \(-2(x-1) -2(y-1) + 0(z-0) = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 2\). For \(D(1,1,1)\): \(1+1=2\), so \(D\) lies on the plane. A student who tries to plug \(D\) into an incorrect equation (e.g., using wrong normal) reveals an inability to compute the cross product correctly or to use the point-normal form.

questions.q: A student writes the equation of a plane through \((2, -1, 3)\) with normal vector \(3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}\) as \(3(x-2) + 4(y-1) - 5(z-3) = 0\). Identify and correct the error.
questions.a: The error is in the \(y\)-term: the point's \(y\)-coordinate is \(-1\), so it should be \(y - (-1) = y+1\), not \(y-1\). The correct equation is \(3(x-2) + 4(y+1) - 5(z-3) = 0\). This mistake shows the student is mechanically applying \(y - y_1\) without substituting the negative coordinate correctly, a very common sign error in board exams.

questions.q: Construct a real-world problem where a plane equation through a given point with a given normal is needed. Provide the point, normal, and ask for the equation. Then modify the problem so that the plane must pass through three given points instead.
questions.a: Example: A solar panel is installed on a roof such that its surface passes through the point \((3, 2, 5)\) (in meters) and is perpendicular to the sun's rays direction vector \(2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}\). Find the plane equation. Modified version: The panel's corners are at \((3,2,5)\), \((5,1,8)\), and \((2,4,7)\). Find the plane equation. A poor answer would give trivial coordinates or collinear points, showing the student doesn't understand the geometric requirement of non-collinearity for three points to define a plane.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A plane in three-dimensional space is uniquely determined if it passes through a given point and has a known normal vector (direction ______ to the plane).
Fill in the blank: To write the equation of this roof plane, we first need a vector ______ to the roof.
Fill in the blank: The key insight is that a plane is completely defined by a point and a normal vector — just as a line in ______D is defined by a point and a slope.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can derive both vector and Cartesian equations of a plane passing through a given point with a specified normal vector, and can also find the equation of a plane passing through three non-collinear points by first determining the normal vector via cross product.
